section_summary: This section documents U.S. and Allied efforts to locate, examine, safeguard, and dispose of Japanese diplomatic archives, official property, and funds after the war. Reports from missions across Europe, the Americas, the Middle East, and Canada describe local holdings and establish Four-Power custody, joint trust accounts, rules for selling official property, and protections for private belongings. A particularly extensive, duplicated despatch from Mexico records negotiations among the American, British, Chinese, and Soviet ambassadors over Japanese archives, assets, relief payments, and property.

subfiles.title: Repeat of circular airgram on Japanese archives to Brussels
subfiles.from: U.S. Secretary of State James F. Byrnes
subfiles.about: Repeats the January 31 circular airgram requested by the Brussels Embassy.
subfiles.summary: The Department responds to Brussels telegram No. 40 of February 8. It retransmits the circular airgram of January 31 concerning Japanese archives and property.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3587 on custody and examination of Japanese archives in Canada
subfiles.from: Ray Atherton, American Embassy, Ottawa, with enclosures from N. A. Robertson and Wm. Wills
subfiles.about: Reports Canadian acquisition of Japanese archives and proposes a joint examination with U.S. and other Allied officials.
subfiles.summary: Canada has received Japanese diplomatic and consular archives from the Swiss protecting power and is assembling material from Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal, and Ottawa. Atherton requests instructions and suggests sending a Japanese-language officer from Washington; the enclosures include Robertson's invitation to participate and a detailed inventory of boxes from the former Japanese consul in Vancouver.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on Canadian custody of Japanese property and archives
subfiles.from: Bishop, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports information given to Japan about Canada's assumption of custody over Japanese archives and property.
subfiles.summary: The Swiss representative informed the Japanese Government that Canada had appointed a custodian for Japanese property and archives. The telegram notes transfers at Vancouver and Montreal and the possibility of a later transfer to the American Ambassador.

subfiles.title: Correction to Tokyo telegram serial number
subfiles.from: Tokyo
subfiles.about: Corrects the serial number of the preceding Tokyo message from 88 to 98.
subfiles.summary: The message states that the telegram received as No. 88 should instead be numbered 98. Its subject is Japanese archives in Canada.

subfiles.title: Instructions to Baghdad on Japanese property and funds
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Sets rules for storing or selling Japanese official property and safeguarding Japanese funds.
subfiles.summary: Official Japanese property should be stored unless deterioration, excessive quantity, or disproportionate expense makes storage impracticable, in which case official property may be sold. Private effects are not to be sold, while public and private funds and sale proceeds are to enter a jointly controlled Allied trust account usable for custodial expenses and approved relief.

subfiles.title: Record-copy notice and duplicate Tokyo telegram on Canadian custody
subfiles.doc_type: record-copy cover sheet and incoming telegram
subfiles.from: Bishop, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Preserves a replacement record copy of the telegram reporting Canadian custody of Japanese archives and property.
subfiles.summary: The cover sheet explains that the attached white copy replaces an action copy not returned to central records. The repeated telegram describes Canada's appointment of a custodian and the transfers at Vancouver and Montreal.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 13,509 on Swedish expenditures for Japanese interests in Chile
subfiles.doc_type: despatch with letter and financial statement
subfiles.from: Hugh Millard, American Embassy, Santiago, with enclosures from Tore Högstedt and Curt Hartzell
subfiles.about: Transmits the Swedish Legation's account of expenditures for protecting Japanese interests in Chile.
subfiles.summary: The Swedish Legation estimates that the allotted 304,544.18 Chilean pesos will cover routine protection through the end of 1946. Its statement lists rent, salaries, premises, telegrams, travel, and miscellaneous costs for November–December 1945, while confirming that extraordinary expenditures such as repatriation require further authorization.

subfiles.title: Prague report on Japanese archives and property
subfiles.from: Laurence A. Steinhardt, American Embassy, Prague
subfiles.about: Reports that no significant Japanese archives or property were found in Czechoslovakia.
subfiles.summary: Steinhardt answers the Department's January 31 circular regarding Japanese archives and property. He refers to an earlier telegram and states that no Japanese property of consequence was found in the country.

subfiles.title: Beirut report on prior examination of Japanese archives
subfiles.from: Gordon H. Mattison, American Legation, Beirut
subfiles.about: States that earlier Beirut despatches already supplied the requested inventory and examination results.
subfiles.summary: The Legation had previously inventoried Japanese consular property and summarized records in French and English. A Japanese-language scholar had also examined the Japanese records, so Mattison considers further action unnecessary.

subfiles.title: Rome telegram proposing a Four-Power examination at Villa Berlingieri
subfiles.from: Alexander C. Kirk, American Embassy, Rome
subfiles.about: Describes the former Japanese Embassy premises and proposes using military Japanese-language personnel to inspect its contents.
subfiles.summary: A preliminary visit found numerous rooms, cases, safes, furnishings, publications, personal effects, and a wine cellar at Villa Berlingieri. Because the American and British embassies lacked staff, Kirk proposed that the Joint Diplomatic Research Agency use Japanese-speaking military personnel and that the villa's top floor remain rented for a Four-Power investigation.

subfiles.title: Department instructions on financing the Rome archive examination
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Authorizes exploration of rental and staffing arrangements for examining the former Japanese Embassy in Rome.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy is told to determine the rent for continued occupation and consider paying costs by selling office furniture, household goods, and wine. The War Department has no objection to using qualified military personnel locally for archive work if the theater commander agrees.

subfiles.title: Moscow Airgram A-84 declining action on the circular
subfiles.from: George F. Kennan, American Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.about: Assumes that the Moscow Embassy need take no action on the Japanese-archives circular.
subfiles.summary: Kennan refers to the January 31 circular and an earlier Embassy telegram. In light of the previously reported circumstances, he assumes no current action is required.

subfiles.title: Department concurrence with Moscow's no-action position
subfiles.from: U.S. Secretary of State James F. Byrnes
subfiles.about: Concurs that Moscow need not act immediately but preserves U.S. interest in future access.
subfiles.summary: The Department agrees that the Embassy need take no action under the circular at present. It nevertheless asks the Embassy to participate in examining Japanese documents if access later becomes practicable.

subfiles.title: Instructions to Cairo on Japanese premises, property, and funds
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Approves storage and disposal arrangements for Japanese property and the former legation premises in Cairo.
subfiles.summary: Private property is to be warehoused, with charges paid from official-property sale proceeds or rent. The Department approves action regarding archives, sales, and rental of the former legation, with income deposited in a joint trust account for storage and custodial expenses.

subfiles.title: San Salvador Despatch No. 738 on Japanese archives and blocked funds
subfiles.from: John F. Simmons, American Embassy, San Salvador
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese archives contained little of interest and identifies a blocked Japanese account in El Salvador.
subfiles.summary: The few archives received from the Spanish Legation contained no significant correspondence or cryptographic material. The Embassy discovered 9,020 colones in a blocked account, apparently relief money and automobile-sale proceeds, and asked the Salvadoran Foreign Ministry how the funds should be disposed of.

subfiles.title: Department instruction on the blocked Japanese funds in El Salvador
subfiles.from: U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge, American Mission, San Salvador
subfiles.about: Advises against pressing El Salvador to transfer the small blocked Japanese account if its government objects.
subfiles.summary: The Department considers the 9,020-colón balance insignificant for reparations purposes. If El Salvador declines to transfer it to the Four Allied Powers, the Embassy should not press, provided the Salvadoran Government takes no final action before broader Japanese external-asset policy is settled.

subfiles.title: Brussels request for the November 16 circular telegram
subfiles.from: Richard C. Patterson Jr., American Embassy, Brussels
subfiles.about: Requests expedited transmission of the missing November 16 circular on Japanese archives and property.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy acknowledges receipt of the repeated January 31 circular. It reports that it still lacks the November 16 circular telegram and asks the Department to expedite it.

subfiles.title: Department transmission of the November 16 circular to Brussels
subfiles.from: U.S. Secretary of State James F. Byrnes
subfiles.about: Responds to Brussels by repeating the requested circular on reports concerning Japanese archives and property.
subfiles.summary: The Department answers Brussels telegram No. 226. It transmits the November 16, 1945 circular concerning submission of reports on Japanese archives and property.

subfiles.title: Lisbon request for urgent property-disposal instructions
subfiles.doc_type: incoming telegram with duplicate information copy
subfiles.from: Herman B. Baruch, American Embassy, Lisbon
subfiles.about: Requests immediate guidance because storage charges on Japanese property are accumulating.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy has received no answer to the Allied Committee recommendations forwarded in December 1945. British and Chinese authorities favor a public sale, and Baruch asks urgently how to dispose of the property while warehouse charges continue to mount.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Lisbon on sale and storage of Japanese property
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Authorizes sale of official Japanese property when storage is impracticable while protecting archives and private effects.
subfiles.summary: The Department says detailed answers are being sent by airmail. Official property may be sold if it cannot practicably be stored, with proceeds entering a joint trust account, but former officials' personal property and official archives are excluded from sale.

subfiles.title: Request to SCAP for Japanese implementing instructions and reports
subfiles.from: U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Requests copies of Japanese Government instructions implementing MacArthur's directive on diplomatic records and property.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks SCAP to mail copies of all Japanese instructions implementing the October 25, 1945 directive. It also requests any available reports describing action taken by recipients of those instructions.

subfiles.title: Notification to SCAP that Canada has assumed custody
subfiles.from: U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo, for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: States that no further action is needed on the earlier request concerning Japanese archives in Canada.
subfiles.summary: The Department has learned that Canada received the archives directly from the Swiss protecting power. It therefore withdraws the need for action under the earlier telegram.

subfiles.title: Geist covering letter on Four-Power negotiations in Mexico
subfiles.from: Raymond H. Geist
subfiles.to: John Carrigan, Division of Mexican Affairs
subfiles.about: Transmits the Mexico despatch and privately describes disagreements with the Soviet representative over archives and relief payments.
subfiles.summary: Geist highlights the difficulty of negotiating with the Soviet ambassador and argues that a potentially important file of Japanese-German correspondence should be kept at the American Embassy rather than the Soviet Embassy. He also reports conflicting instructions to the Swedish Minister concerning continued relief payments to Japanese nationals in Mexico.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 28,703 and memorandum on Japanese assets in Mexico
subfiles.from: Raymond H. Geist, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Records the Four-Power ambassadors' negotiations over Japanese property, funds, archives, and relief expenditures in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The American, British, Chinese, and Soviet ambassadors agreed in principle to auction official property, protect identifiable private effects, and place funds and sale proceeds in a jointly controlled Bank of Mexico account. They appointed a subcommittee to investigate relief payments, terminate expenses, arrange the sale, and examine the archives with Chinese and Soviet Japanese-language readers. The memorandum also records disagreement over the archives' place of custody, preparations for a formal transfer from Swedish Minister Herbert de Ribbing, and a request that any code books be copied immediately.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Despatch No. 28,703 and its meeting memorandum
subfiles.from: Raymond H. Geist, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Duplicates the detailed report of the February 27 Four-Power meeting concerning Japanese assets in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: This clean duplicate repeats the agreements to sell official property, retain identifiable private effects, and deposit Japanese funds in a joint account. It also repeats the creation of a four-member subcommittee, the proposed transfer from the Swedish Minister, competing preferences over archive custody, and arrangements for Japanese-language examination and copying any code books.

subfiles.title: Brussels telegram on proposed sale or lease of Japanese Embassy property
subfiles.from: Richard C. Patterson Jr., American Embassy, Brussels
subfiles.about: Requests U.S. views on a Soviet proposal to acquire former Japanese Embassy property in Brussels.
subfiles.summary: At a Four-Power meeting the Soviet mission renewed its wish to purchase the Japanese Embassy building and furniture, while the British favored sale or lease according to local conditions. Patterson asks for instructions on the real estate, furniture, and boxes of private property, noting that a separate archive report will follow.

subfiles.title: Baghdad Airgram A-58 referring to safe-opening report
subfiles.from: Koose, American Legation, Baghdad
subfiles.about: Directs the Department to an earlier despatch describing the opening of a safe in the former Japanese Legation.
subfiles.summary: The Legation responds to Department Airgram A-17. It states that the report on opening the Baghdad safe is contained in Despatch No. 1043 of January 18, 1946.

subfiles.title: Bogotá telegram on Japanese assets and archives
subfiles.from: John C. Wiley, American Embassy, Bogotá
subfiles.about: Requests instructions on dividing Japanese liquid assets and handling archives stored at the British Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Japanese liquid assets total slightly more than 100,000 pesos, and the Soviet minister proposes a four-way division including China. The Soviet representative also suggests photographing the archives, but Wiley believes they contain little of interest and proposes Colonel Fonoff as permanent custodian.

subfiles.title: Department response to Bogotá on microfilming and joint custody
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Bogotá, for John C. Wiley
subfiles.about: Instructs Bogotá to preserve access to useful archives and place Japanese liquid assets in a joint trustee account.
subfiles.summary: Archives or selected portions judged important should be microfilmed or photographed for Department examination. The Embassy is asked to explain its changed assessment of the records, retain access in the meantime, and deposit liquid assets in a joint trustee account pending final disposition.

subfiles.title: Unsent alternate draft to Bogotá
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Presents an unsent alternative response concerning photography, custody, and liquid Japanese assets.
subfiles.summary: The draft raises no objection to photographing the archives but warns that the cost may be prohibitive. It calls for continued custody and placement of liquid assets in a joint trustee account, but the copy is marked “NOT SENT.”

subfiles.title: Memorandum of telephone conversation on Japanese property in Siam
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, Special Projects Division
subfiles.about: Records interdivisional discussion about informing the British Embassy of planned action in Siam.
subfiles.summary: Lacy advised Williams of a draft telegram directing Bangkok to form a British-Chinese-American committee to receive Japanese official property and archives from the Siamese Government. They agreed that Lacy would notify Iverson at the British Embassy in Washington.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter and Foreign Office circular on Japanese archives and property
subfiles.from: G. R. Ranken, British Embassy, Washington
subfiles.to: A. E. Clattenburg Jr., U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Provides British policy for disposing of Japanese diplomatic archives, official property, and private effects outside the Western Hemisphere.
subfiles.summary: The circular permits examination and later destruction or transfer of unimportant archives, calls for ending leases and selling Japanese government buildings and movable official property, and places proceeds in Four-Power accounts. Stamps, seals, flags, insignia, and propaganda require special handling, while private belongings cannot be finally disposed of without authority from their owners or the responsible U.S. authorities. It also treats Manchukuo property as potentially an internal Chinese matter.

subfiles.title: Helsinki telegram on disposal of Japanese Legation property
subfiles.doc_type: incoming telegram with duplicate action copy
subfiles.from: Hulley, American Legation, Helsinki
subfiles.about: Reports an Allied plan to open safes, secure archives, warehouse private effects, and dispose of official Japanese property in Finland.
subfiles.summary: American, British, and Soviet officials agreed to open the safes, seal archives and codes, and store them at the U.S. Legation while warehousing private property commercially. Because goods were scarce and Finnish currency weak, they proposed allowing each legation to select appraised items against its national share and selling the remainder before the lease expired.

subfiles.title: Department objection to dividing Japanese property in Helsinki
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Approves custody measures but rejects uncompensated division of Japanese official property among Allied missions.
subfiles.summary: The Department accepts the proposed handling of archives and private property. It considers division of official property inconsistent with Four-Power custodial responsibility, although missions may rent or purchase desired items if adequate compensation is paid into a joint trust account.

subfiles.title: Rome Airgram A-72 on the probable destruction of Japanese archives
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Rome
subfiles.about: Concludes that Japanese officials probably destroyed nearly all valuable archives in Italy before Rome's liberation.
subfiles.summary: Empty safes and filing cabinets and cases of printed publications suggest that little useful material remains at the former Japanese Embassy. An Italian custodian reported that Japanese officials spent about eight months organizing effects and destroying papers, while U.S. consulates in Florence, Milan, Palermo, and Genoa found no significant surviving Japanese official archives or property.

subfiles.title: Havana Despatch No. 1294 and memorandum on photographed registration cards
subfiles.doc_type: despatch with memorandum and photographic-enclosure list
subfiles.from: Robert F. Woodward, American Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: Transmits photographs of selected Japanese Legation registration cards for further intelligence examination.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy photographed twelve registration cards concerning Japanese individuals whose activities, whereabouts, or recall to Japan might be important. Because the Cuban Japanese-language readers may not have interpreted them completely or accurately, copies were also supplied to the Embassy's military, naval, and legal attachés for forwarding to their departments.
